### 3 Chemical bonding - Structured Questions: Easy

::: {.question-card}
### Example 1 · Intermolecular forces · 1.3 SQ Easy Q1

**(a)** Name the three main types of intermolecular force and arrange them in increasing order of strength. `[2 marks]`

**(b)** Methanol, $\ce{CH3OH}$, is a small polar molecule. Describe how two methanol molecules form a hydrogen bond. Include the partial charges and the lone pair involved. `[3 marks]`

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ul><li><strong>(a)</strong> London dispersion forces, permanent dipole--permanent dipole forces, hydrogen bonds, in that order.</li><li><strong>(b)</strong> Oxygen is $\delta-$ and the O--H hydrogen is $\delta+$. The $\delta+$ hydrogen is attracted to a lone pair on the oxygen atom of a neighbouring molecule. A hydrogen bond is shown as a dashed line.</li></ul></details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Example 2 · Hydrogen bonding in water and ammonia · 1.3 SQ Easy Q2

Ammonia is very soluble in water.

**(a)** State why ammonia is polar. `[2 marks]`

**(b)** Describe two possible hydrogen bonds between one water molecule and one ammonia molecule. `[4 marks]`

**(c)** State one physical property of ammonia caused by its polarity. `[1 mark]`

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ul><li><strong>(a)</strong> N--H bonds are polar and the molecule is trigonal pyramidal, so the bond dipoles do not cancel.</li><li><strong>(b)</strong> A water $\delta+$ H can hydrogen-bond to the lone pair on N; an ammonia $\delta+$ H can hydrogen-bond to a lone pair on O. Partial charges and the dashed attractions must be shown correctly.</li><li><strong>(c)</strong> It is soluble in water, or has a higher boiling point than a similar non-polar molecule.</li></ul></details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Example 3 · Dot-and-cross diagrams · 1.3 SQ Easy Q3

Draw dot-and-cross diagrams for $\ce{H2}$, $\ce{Cl2}$ and $\ce{HCl}$.

**(a)** Show the bonding pair and all lone pairs. `[3 marks]`

**(b)** Explain why the H--Cl bond is polar. `[2 marks]`

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ul><li><strong>(a)</strong> Each molecule must have one shared pair. $\ce{H2}$ has no lone pairs; each chlorine in $\ce{Cl2}$ has three lone pairs; chlorine in $\ce{HCl}$ has three lone pairs.</li><li><strong>(b)</strong> Chlorine is more electronegative than hydrogen, so the bonding pair is closer to chlorine, giving $\ce{H^{\delta+}-Cl^{\delta-}}$.</li></ul></details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Example 4 · Shapes and bond angles · 1.3 SQ Easy Q4

For each species, state the number of bonding pairs, number of lone pairs on the central atom, shape and approximate bond angle: $\ce{CO2}$, $\ce{BF3}$, $\ce{CH4}$, $\ce{NH3}$ and $\ce{H2O}$. `[10 marks]`

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ul><li>$\ce{CO2}$: 2 regions, 0 lone pairs, linear, $180^\circ$.</li><li>$\ce{BF3}$: 3 bonding pairs, 0 lone pairs, trigonal planar, $120^\circ$.</li><li>$\ce{CH4}$: 4 bonding pairs, 0 lone pairs, tetrahedral, $109.5^\circ$.</li><li>$\ce{NH3}$: 3 bonding pairs, 1 lone pair, trigonal pyramidal, about $107^\circ$.</li><li>$\ce{H2O}$: 2 bonding pairs, 2 lone pairs, bent, about $104.5^\circ$.</li></ul></details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Example 5 · Ionic bonding and physical properties · 1.3 SQ Easy Q5

Sodium chloride is a giant ionic lattice.

**(a)** Describe the structure of solid sodium chloride. `[2 marks]`

**(b)** Explain why solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity but molten sodium chloride does. `[2 marks]`

**(c)** Explain why sodium chloride has a high melting point. `[1 mark]`

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ul><li><strong>(a)</strong> A regular three-dimensional lattice of oppositely charged $\ce{Na+}$ and $\ce{Cl-}$ ions; each ion is surrounded by ions of opposite charge.</li><li><strong>(b)</strong> Solid ions are fixed, whereas molten ions are mobile and can carry charge.</li><li><strong>(c)</strong> Strong electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions require much energy to overcome.</li></ul></details>
:::



### 3 Chemical bonding - Structured Questions: Medium

::: {.question-card}
### Example 8 · Equilibrium and shape of $\ce{PCl3}$ · 1.3 SQ Medium Q1

The equilibrium is:

$$\ce{PCl5(g) <=> PCl3(g) + Cl2(g)}$$

The yield of $\ce{PCl3}$ increases as temperature increases.

**(a)** State whether the forward reaction is endothermic or exothermic and explain. `[2 marks]`

**(b)** State the shape and bond angle around phosphorus in $\ce{PCl3}$. `[2 marks]`

**(c)** Explain why the bond angle is less than $109.5^\circ$. `[2 marks]`

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ul><li><strong>(a)</strong> Endothermic; increasing temperature shifts equilibrium in the endothermic direction and increases the product yield.</li><li><strong>(b)</strong> Trigonal pyramidal; approximately $107^\circ$.</li><li><strong>(c)</strong> There are three bonding pairs and one lone pair. Lone-pair--bond-pair repulsion is stronger than bond-pair--bond-pair repulsion and compresses the angle.</li></ul></details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Example 9 · Polarity and properties of ammonia · 1.3 SQ Medium Q2

**(a)** Explain the meaning of bond polarity using ammonia as an example. `[2 marks]`

**(b)** Explain why the ammonia molecule is polar. `[1 mark]`

**(c)** State one physical property of ammonia caused by its polarity. `[1 mark]`

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ul><li><strong>(a)</strong> Nitrogen is more electronegative than hydrogen, so the shared electron pair in each N--H bond is displaced towards N, giving partial charges.</li><li><strong>(b)</strong> Ammonia is trigonal pyramidal, so the three N--H bond dipoles do not cancel.</li><li><strong>(c)</strong> High solubility in water, or a relatively high boiling point compared with a similar non-polar molecule.</li></ul></details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Example 10 · Bonding in ammonium chloride · 1.3 SQ Medium Q3

When ammonia gas reacts with hydrogen chloride, solid ammonium chloride forms.

**(a)** State the types of bond present within one formula unit of $\ce{NH4Cl}$. `[3 marks]`

**(b)** State how many of each bond type are present if the coordinate bond is shown separately. `[3 marks]`

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ul><li><strong>(a)</strong> Ionic attraction between $\ce{NH4+}$ and $\ce{Cl-}$; covalent N--H bonds within ammonium; one of the N--H bonds is coordinate.</li><li><strong>(b)</strong> One ionic attraction type, four N--H covalent bonds in the ammonium ion, with one formed originally as a coordinate bond. The coordinate bond is chemically equivalent to the other N--H bonds after formation.</li></ul></details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Example 11 · Surface tension and hydrogen bonding · 1.3 SQ Medium Q4

A paperclip can float on water, but sinks after a small amount of soap is added.

Explain both observations in terms of intermolecular forces. `[3 marks]`

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><p>Water has high surface tension caused by hydrogen bonding between water molecules. The surface can support the paperclip if it is placed carefully. Soap disrupts the hydrogen-bond network and lowers surface tension, so the paperclip sinks.</p></details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Example 12 · Comparing boiling points · 1.3 SQ Medium Q5

Compare the boiling points of $\ce{F2}$ and $\ce{HCl}$.

**(a)** Identify the intermolecular forces present in each substance. `[2 marks]`

**(b)** Predict which has the lower boiling point. `[1 mark]`

**(c)** Explain the difference. `[3 marks]`

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ul><li><strong>(a)</strong> Both have London dispersion forces; HCl also has permanent dipole--permanent dipole forces.</li><li><strong>(b)</strong> $\ce{F2}$ has the lower boiling point.</li><li><strong>(c)</strong> HCl has stronger intermolecular attractions because it is polar, so more energy is required to separate its molecules.</li></ul></details>
:::


### 3 Chemical bonding - Structured Questions: Hard

::: {.question-card}
### Example 14 · Nitrate ion and resonance · 1.3 SQ Hard Q1

The nitrate ion is $\ce{NO3-}$.

**(a)** Calculate the total number of valence electrons in one nitrate ion. `[2 marks]`

**(b)** Describe how the electrons are arranged in a valid dot-and-cross structure. `[3 marks]`

**(c)** Explain why the three N--O bonds are equivalent in the real ion. `[2 marks]`

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ul><li><strong>(a)</strong> N contributes 5, three O atoms contribute 18 and the negative charge contributes one: total 24 electrons.</li><li><strong>(b)</strong> N is central, three O atoms are attached, the ion is placed in square brackets with a $1-$ charge, and the octet/charge arrangement is shown correctly. Equivalent resonance structures can be drawn with the double bond in different positions.</li><li><strong>(c)</strong> The actual ion is a resonance hybrid; the bonding electrons are delocalised over all three N--O bonds.</li></ul></details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Example 15 · Methanamide shape and angles · 1.3 SQ Hard Q2

Methanamide has formula $\ce{HCONH2}$.

**(a)** State the shape and approximate bond angle around the carbon atom. `[2 marks]`

**(b)** State the shape and approximate bond angle around the nitrogen atom. `[2 marks]`

**(c)** Explain why the two shapes are different. `[2 marks]`

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ul><li><strong>(a)</strong> The carbonyl carbon has three regions of electron density, so it is trigonal planar, about $120^\circ$.</li><li><strong>(b)</strong> Nitrogen has three bonding pairs and one lone pair, so it is trigonal pyramidal, about $107^\circ$.</li><li><strong>(c)</strong> The nitrogen lone pair gives four electron regions and stronger lone-pair repulsion; the carbon atom has three regions and no lone pair.</li></ul></details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Example 16 · Coordinate bonds and expanded octets · 1.3 SQ Hard Q3

**(a)** Explain how $\ce{PCl6-}$ can form from $\ce{PCl5}$ and $\ce{Cl-}$. `[3 marks]`

**(b)** State the shape of $\ce{PCl6-}$ and justify it using electron-pair repulsion. `[2 marks]`

**(c)** Explain why nitrogen cannot form $\ce{NCl5}$. `[2 marks]`

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ul><li><strong>(a)</strong> A lone pair on $\ce{Cl-}$ is donated to electron-deficient P, forming a coordinate P--Cl bond and the ion $\ce{PCl6-}$.</li><li><strong>(b)</strong> Octahedral; six bonding pairs repel equally and occupy positions as far apart as possible.</li><li><strong>(c)</strong> Nitrogen is a Period 2 atom with no available d orbitals and cannot expand its octet beyond eight electrons.</li></ul></details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Example 17 · Intermolecular forces between water and ammonia · 1.3 SQ Hard Q4

Water and ammonia can form hydrogen bonds with each other.

**(a)** Draw or describe the partial charges on $\ce{H2O}$ and $\ce{NH3}$. `[2 marks]`

**(b)** Describe both possible directions of hydrogen bonding between the two molecules. `[4 marks]`

**(c)** Explain why these interactions make ammonia highly soluble in water. `[2 marks]`

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ul><li><strong>(a)</strong> O and N are $\delta-$; bonded H atoms are $\delta+$.</li><li><strong>(b)</strong> Water H can donate a hydrogen bond to the lone pair on N. Ammonia H can donate a hydrogen bond to a lone pair on O. Both attractions should be shown with dashed lines.</li><li><strong>(c)</strong> Strong attractions form between ammonia and water molecules, replacing some water--water and ammonia--ammonia attractions and allowing the molecules to mix.</li></ul></details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Example 18 · Solid $\ce{PCl5}$ and liquid $\ce{SbCl5}$ · 1.3 SQ Hard Q5

Solid phosphorus(V) chloride has a higher melting point than liquid antimony(V) chloride.

**(a)** State the particles and bonding in solid $\ce{PCl5}$. `[2 marks]`

**(b)** State the particles and intermolecular forces in liquid $\ce{SbCl5}$. `[2 marks]`

**(c)** Explain the difference in melting points. `[3 marks]`

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ul><li><strong>(a)</strong> Solid $\ce{PCl5}$ contains $\ce{PCl4+}$ and $\ce{PCl6-}$ ions in a giant ionic lattice with strong ionic attractions.</li><li><strong>(b)</strong> Liquid $\ce{SbCl5}$ contains covalent molecules held together by relatively weak intermolecular forces.</li><li><strong>(c)</strong> More energy is needed to overcome strong ionic attractions in solid $\ce{PCl5}$ than weak intermolecular forces between $\ce{SbCl5}$ molecules.</li></ul></details>
:::
